text: Theodore von Kármán (Hungarian: (szőlőskislaki) Kármán Tódor [(sølløːʃkiʃlɒki) ˈkaːrmaːn ˈtoːdor]; 11 May 1881 – 6 May 1963) was a Hungarian-American mathematician, aerospace engineer, and physicist known for his key advances in aerodynamics, particularly in supersonic and hypersonic airflow characterization, and is regarded as the outstanding aerodynamic theoretician of the twentieth century. Born into a Jewish family in Budapest, Austria-Hungary, he was the son of Helen (Kohn or Konn, Hungarian: Kohn Ilka) and Mór Kármán, with one ancestor being Rabbi Judah Loew ben Bezalel. He studied engineering at the Royal Joseph Technical University, now known as Budapest University of Technology and Economics, and after graduating in 1902, moved to the German Empire to join Ludwig Prandtl at the University of Göttingen, where he earned his doctorate in 1908 and taught for four years. In 1912, he became director of the Aeronautical Institute at RWTH Aachen University, one of Germany’s leading institutions, though his tenure was interrupted by service in the Austro-Hungarian Army from 1915 to 1918, during which he designed the Petróczy-Kármán-Žurovec, an early helicopter. After the war, he returned to Aachen with his mother and sister Josephine de Karman, who encouraged him to expand his scientific influence beyond national borders; they organized the first international conference in mechanics in September 1922 in Innsbruck, leading to the formation of the International Union of Theoretical and Applied Mechanics. Kármán left RWTH Aachen in 1930. Concerned about European developments, he accepted the directorship of the Guggenheim Aeronautical Laboratory at the California Institute of Technology (GALCIT) in 1930, appointing Frank Wattendorf as his research assistant. His student Ernest Edwin Sechler, with Kármán’s support, developed an understanding of aeroelasticity for reliable airframes. In 1936, Kármán formed the Aerojet Corporation with graduate student Frank Malina and collaborator Jack Parsons to manufacture JATO rocket motors, later becoming a naturalized U.S. citizen. During World War II, U.S. military interest in rocket research grew due to German advances; in early 1943, the U.S. Army Air Forces received reports from British intelligence about German rockets capable of traveling over 100 miles (160 km), and Kármán provided an analysis in a letter dated 2 August 1943. In 1944, he and others affiliated with GALCIT founded the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), now a federally funded research and development center managed by Caltech under NASA. In 1946, he became the first chairman of the Scientific Advisory Group for the U.S. Army Air Forces and helped establish AGARD (1951), the International Council of the Aeronautical Sciences (1956), the International Academy of Astronautics (1960), and the Von Karman Institute for Fluid Dynamics in Brussels (1956). He was instrumental in recognizing the importance of swept-back wings in modern jet aircraft and made significant contributions to theories of non-elastic buckling, unsteady wakes in circum-cylinder flow, stability of laminar flow, turbulence, airfoils in steady and unsteady flow, boundary layers, and supersonic aerodynamics, as well as to elasticity, vibration, heat transfer, and crystallography. In June 1944, Kármán underwent surgery for intestinal cancer in New York City, which caused two hernias and resulted in a slow recovery; in September, while still in New York, he met U.S. Army Air Forces Commanding General Henry H. Arnold on a runway at LaGuardia Airport, who proposed that Kármán move to Washington, D.C. to lead the Scientific Advisory Group and serve as a long-range planning consultant. Kármán returned to Pasadena in mid-September, was appointed to the SAG position on October 23, 1944, and left Caltech in December 1944. At age 81, he received the first National Medal of Science in a White House ceremony by President John F. Kennedy, recognized for his leadership in aeronautical science and engineering, effective teaching, distinguished counsel to the Armed Services, and promotion of international cooperation in science and engineering. Kármán never married; he died on a trip to Aachen, Germany, in 1963, and his body was returned to the United States to be entombed in the Beth Olam Mausoleum at Hollywood Forever Cemetery. He has sometimes been described as one of The Martians. His fame stemmed from using mathematical tools to study fluid flow and interpreting results to guide practical designs. His autobiography, *The Wind and Beyond*, published in 1965 by Lee Edson with Little, Brown and Company, received enthusiastic reviews from J. Kestin, who advised readers to study it as a reference, while Charles Süsskind criticized it for lacking engagement with Wernher von Braun’s arrival in America and the Hsue-shen Tsien affair, and labeled Kármán a militarist due to his lifelong association with military authorities. Sydney Goldstein, who wrote the Royal Society memoir, remembered Kármán as a warm-hearted, witty, internationally recognized engineer and scientist who found the military to be the most comfortable group to work with. On creativity, Kármán wrote that the finest creative thought arises from the quiet of one’s own world, and I. B. Holley noted his penetrating insights into the creative process, while also noting his fondness for convivial drinking and the company of beautiful women.
